title: Ansel and the House
premise: Folklorist Rosalind Oyelaran returns to his late grandmother's house in the village of Hollowmere to record the funeral songs no one will sing twice, only to find that every photograph taken inside now contains an extra chair — and, increasingly, someone sitting in it. The house was never empty: decades ago, his grandmother invited something in to save her family from a famine-winter, and that bargain is coming due with the estate's final signing. As Rosalind pieces together the truth from suppressed songs and buried ledgers, he must survive one night in the house until sunrise, when the last resident — himself, by inheritance — either signs the papers renewing the invitation or breaks it. He burns the papers at dawn, freeing the village but erasing every memory anyone holds of his grandmother, paying survival's price in remembrance.
about_author: Sable Delacroix is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal villages before turning to horror. They write about houses that remember and the bargains families make to keep their names off the ledger.

chapters.title: The Song Nobody Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Recording folk songs in Hollowmere, Rosalind notices the villagers stop mid-verse whenever a certain lullaby surfaces, and an old woman warns him not to go back to his grandmother's house. Beat: unease planted beneath professional detachment.

chapters.title: Five Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. On the drive to the house, Rosalind reviews five years of rationalizations for childhood noises — settling pipes, foxes, memory. A letter from the solicitor about the estate sits on the passenger seat. Beat: the armor of reason established.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Unpacking photographs for the memorial display, Rosalind finds a wooden chair in every image that was never there — sometimes empty, once occupied by a blurred figure. Beat: first undeniable crack in the rational world.

chapters.title: Keys That Don't Fit
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Exploring the house, Rosalind finds doors to rooms he remembers being larger, a staircase with one step too many, and a key ring labeled in his grandmother's hand: DO NOT USE AFTER DARK. Beat: the house resists being known.

chapters.title: The Solicitor's Silence
chapters.summary: Solicitor Mr. Vane's POV. Vane arrives with the inheritance papers but refuses to enter past the threshold, leaving documents on the porch and urging Rosalind to sign quickly, before 'the term ends.' Beat: outside confirmation that something is scheduled.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Kept
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In the attic, Rosalind finds his grandmother's household ledger; entries from the famine winter shift from grain counts to names crossed out, ending with a line in Latin: 'invitatus est.' Beat: the bargain's existence surfaces.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Won't Look
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind visits neighbor Edith Marsh, who fed him as a child; she answers questions about the house only while facing away from it, and begs him to sign whatever Vane brought. Beat: the village's complicity revealed.

chapters.title: Second Verse, Forbidden
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Deciphering the forbidden lullaby from his recordings, Rosalind realizes it is an instruction manual — a binding song describing how something was welcomed in and how it might be kept waiting. Beat: folklore becomes procedure.

chapters.title: It Sat Down
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At dusk, the extra chair appears physically in the parlor, pulled up to the table as if for dinner. Cold moves through the rooms like a tide. Beat: the metaphor takes up space.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith recalls the winter of 1963, when children starved and Rosalind's grandmother walked into the dark with a lantern and came back with food — and a guest nobody saw. Beat: sympathy braided with dread.

chapters.title: The Papers on the Porch
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Reading the inheritance papers, Rosalind finds clauses that aren't property law: terms of hospitality, renewal periods, a signature line that seems to warm under his hand. Beat: temptation formalized.

chapters.title: Photographs With Company
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. New photos Rosalind takes show the seated figure closer each time — a tall, patient shape whose face resolves slightly more in every frame. Beat: countdown made visual.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A hidden letter reveals Grandmother Oyelaran knew she was dying and arranged for the house to pass to Rosalind deliberately — either to renew the protection or end it, her final act of trust. Beat: love entangled with burden.

chapters.title: Vane Returns at Nightfall
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane comes after dark, breaking his own rule, desperate; he confesses his firm has administered the 'tenancy' for generations and that if no resident signs by sunrise, the thing collects broadly. Beat: stakes widen beyond one man.

chapters.title: The House Rearranges
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Corridors lengthen toward the kitchen and shorten toward the exits; windows show the village as it looked during the famine. The house wants him comfortable, or wanting. Beat: architecture as appetite.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Part Two
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith admits she helped choose which neighbors' names went into the ledger that winter — including Rosalind's grandfather's. Her guilt has kept her facing away for fifty years. Beat: power's corruption given a human face.

chapters.title: Dinner Is Set
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind wakes to a laid table: three places, hot food he didn't cook, and the chair drawn out for him. Eating feels like signing. He throws the plate into the hearth. Beat: refusal and its immediate cost — the lights die.

chapters.title: The Voice in the Walls
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The presence begins speaking in his grandmother's voice, then his mother's, offering warmth, family, an end to loneliness. Rosalind nearly answers aloud. Beat: the temptation turns intimate.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Cross-referencing ledger and song, Rosalind reconstructs the truth: his grandmother invited a hunger-spirit in as a guest, and guests must be hosted or dismissed — dismissal requires the truth spoken aloud by a resident. Beat: the win condition clarified.

chapters.title: The Village at the Windows
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Villagers gather outside in the dark, faces blank, humming the forbidden lullaby — they have come to see the tenancy renewed, their safety purchased with his signature. Beat: betrayal by the protected.

chapters.title: Midnight: First Term
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The house enforces its rules: doors vanish, the cold deepens, and the figure in the photographs is now standing behind him in mirrors. Rosalind anchors himself by reading the ledger aloud. Beat: endurance begins.

chapters.title: One A.M.: The Kind Host
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The presence shifts tactics, showing Rosalind tender false memories — birthdays, lullabies, a childhood the house curated. Grief becomes the weapon. Beat: sorrow weaponized against him.

chapters.title: Two A.M.: Vane's Bargain
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Trapped in the house too, Vane offers Rosalind an escape clause: sign and live comfortably elsewhere while a proxy tenant suffers. Rosalind sees exactly how power corrupts — it always finds a middleman. Beat: moral crux.

chapters.title: Three A.M.: The Chair Moves
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The extra chair drags itself to sit directly behind Rosalind wherever he stands. He stops turning around. The truth he must speak requires naming what his grandmother did — and forgiving her. Beat: physical dread, emotional preparation.

chapters.title: Four A.M.: Edith at the Door
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith breaks fifty years of avoidance and enters the house to stand with Rosalind, facing it at last, adding her testimony of the original invitation. Beat: courage as penance.

chapters.title: The Figure Has a Face
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In the final photograph, the figure's face resolves: it wears his grandmother's expression, hollowed — the house wearing the dead to be let in. Rosalind grieves and hardens. Beat: the cruelest illusion.

chapters.title: Five A.M.: The Signature Warms
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The papers appear in his hands unbidden, the pen already uncapped, his name half-written in ink that isn't ink. He burns them in the cold hearth, which flares without wood. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: The House Objects
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Enraged, the house collapses inward — walls breathing, floors tilting toward the parlor where the chair waits. Edith recites the lullaby's second verse as a countersong. Beat: climax opens.

chapters.title: Six A.M.: Speaking the Truth
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Standing in the parlor, Rosalind speaks the whole truth aloud: the famine, the invitation, the names traded, his grandmother's desperate love and terrible price. The house screams through every room. Beat: climax.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Light enters where windows used to be. The presence departs not violently but like a guest finally released, taking the warmth of every memory of Grandmother Oyelaran with it. Rosalind forgets her face mid-farewell. Beat: victory priced in grief.

chapters.title: The Empty Photographs
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Every photograph is now ordinary — and in none of them does his grandmother appear. Edith remembers nothing of 1963. Only Rosalind, who spoke the truth, retains the burden. Beat: isolation of the knower.

chapters.title: A Village That Slept Well
chapters.summary: Multiple villagers' POVs. Hollowmere wakes refreshed, prosperous, vaguely grateful, unable to say why. No one hums the lullaby because no one knows it. Beat: the corruption of comfortable forgetting.

chapters.title: Vane's New Client File
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane archives the Hollowmere file and opens another: a house in the next county, a dying resident, papers to prepare. The machinery continues. Beat: systemic evil persists.

chapters.title: What Rosalind Keeps
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind finds one artifact the house missed: a recording of his grandmother singing the forbidden song, made years ago. He cannot remember her, but he can hear her. Beat: grief transmuted into preservation.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Signs Nothing
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind sells the house to a young family, telling them nothing except: keep the receipts, count your chairs, and never sing a song you don't understand all the way through. Beat: passing on vigilance instead of curse.

chapters.title: Archive Notes
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Back at his university archive, Rosalind catalogs the Hollowmere recordings under a sealed restriction: to be opened only by someone who has counted an extra chair. Beat: turning trauma into guardianship.

chapters.title: Edith's Grave
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind buries Edith's confession letter with her at her request, the only witness honored. On the headstone he carves no dates — she asked to be remembered as facing forward. Beat: redemption closed gently.

chapters.title: The Second Verse, Sung Once
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Alone, Rosalind sings the lullaby's second verse once — the dismissal verse — so it exists in living memory somewhere, then lets it go. The room stays ordinary. Beat: reclaiming the folklore.

chapters.title: Ansel and the House
chapters.summary: Final chapter, framed as a folk tale Rosalind writes. He retells his ordeal as the story of Ansel, who held out until sunrise and paid in remembering. The tale ends: 'And the house stood empty, which is the kindest thing a house can be.' Beat: resolution as myth-making.

chapters.title: Coda: Someone Counts the Chairs
chapters.summary: Epilogue, unnamed POV. Years later, in the sold house, a child counting chairs in old photographs pauses at one image, frowns, and asks her mother why there's an extra seat. The mother doesn't look up. Beat: quiet dread, the cycle listening.
